**Hungarian Revolution of 1956 and Imre Nagy**
A nationwide uprising against the Soviet-backed communist government that began in Budapest in October 1956. Student demonstrators trying to broadcast their demands at the Magyar Radio building were shot by the ÁVH secret police; protesters toppled a giant Stalin statue, leaving only its boots, and freed Cardinal Mindszenty. Reformist prime minister Imre Nagy announced Hungary's withdrawal from the Warsaw Pact, but Soviet tanks crushed the revolution and Nagy was later executed.

**János Kádár and "Goulash Communism"**
Kádár was installed by the Soviets after the 1956 revolution and ruled Hungary until 1988. After harsh early repression, his "Goulash Communism" allowed limited market reforms and consumer goods, which made Hungary known as the "happiest barracks" in the Eastern Bloc.

**Lajos Kossuth and the Revolution of 1848**
Kossuth led Hungary's 1848 revolution and war of independence against the Austrian Habsburgs, which produced the April (March) Laws and the Twelve Points of reform. The young emperor Franz Joseph I called in Tsar Nicholas I of Russia, whose army helped crush the revolt; Artúr Görgei surrendered in 1849, and Kossuth went into exile and toured the United States in 1851.

**Ausgleich of 1867 and the Dual Monarchy**
The "Compromise" that turned the Austrian Empire into Austria-Hungary, a dual monarchy in which Hungary had its own government and parliament but shared a monarch (Franz Joseph I), army, and foreign policy with Austria. The Dual Monarchy dissolved at the end of World War I in 1918.

**Battle of Mohács (1526)**
A crushing defeat of the Hungarian army by Suleiman the Magnificent's Ottoman forces. Commander Pál Tomori was killed and the young King Louis II drowned while fleeing in his armor, and Hungary was afterward divided among the Ottomans, the Habsburgs, and the principality of Transylvania.

**Saint Stephen and the Árpád dynasty**
Stephen I, of the Árpád dynasty descended from the Magyar chieftain Árpád, was crowned Hungary's first king in 1000 with a crown sent by Pope Sylvester II, and he Christianized the country. His father, Grand Prince Géza, had converted earlier. Stephen's preserved right hand, the Holy Dexter, is a relic, and the Holy Crown named for him has a distinctive bent cross.

**Matthias Corvinus and the Black Army**
The Renaissance king of Hungary (reigned 1458–1490) and son of the general John Hunyadi, who had fought the Ottomans and escaped the disastrous Crusade of Varna in 1444. Matthias built the Black Army, one of Europe's first standing mercenary armies, captured Vienna, and collected the Bibliotheca Corviniana, one of Europe's largest libraries; his name comes from the raven on his coat of arms.

**Miklós Horthy and Operation Panzerfaust**
Admiral Horthy was Hungary's regent from 1920 to 1944 and allied it with Nazi Germany in World War II. When he tried to make a separate peace in 1944, German commando Otto Skorzeny kidnapped Horthy's son (reportedly rolled up in a carpet) in Operation Panzerfaust, forcing Horthy to hand power to Ferenc Szálasi of the fascist Arrow Cross Party, which persecuted and murdered Budapest's Jews.

**Raoul Wallenberg**
A Swedish diplomat in Budapest in 1944–1945 who, working with Swiss diplomat Carl Lutz and others, issued protective passports and set up safe houses that saved thousands of Hungarian Jews. He was arrested by the Soviets during the siege of Budapest and disappeared in Soviet custody.

**"Blood in the Water" match**
A violent water polo semifinal at the 1956 Melbourne Olympics, played weeks after the Soviet invasion, in which Hungary beat the Soviet Union 4–0. It became famous after Hungarian player Ervin Zádor left the pool bleeding from a punch.

**Treaty of Trianon (1920)**
The post-World War I peace treaty between the Allies and Hungary that took away about two-thirds of the old Kingdom of Hungary's territory, leaving millions of ethnic Hungarians in neighboring states. Resentment over Trianon shaped interwar Hungarian politics.

**Mátyás Rákosi and "salami tactics"**
The Stalinist leader who took over Hungary after World War II, coining "salami tactics" for eliminating rival parties such as the Smallholders slice by slice. His regime relied on the ÁVH secret police and imprisoned Cardinal József Mindszenty.

**Martyrs of Arad**
Thirteen Hungarian rebel generals executed at Arad in October 1849 after the failed revolution, on the orders of the Austrian general Julius Haynau, called the "Hangman of Arad." According to legend, Austrians clinked beer glasses to celebrate, so Hungarians vowed not to clink beer mugs for 150 years.

**Béla Kun and the Red and White Terrors**
After the 1918 Aster Revolution ended Habsburg rule, Béla Kun set up the short-lived Hungarian Soviet Republic in 1919, whose violence was called the Red Terror. It was overthrown, and forces associated with Miklós Horthy carried out a retaliatory White Terror.

**Battle of Lechfeld (955)**
The battle in which the German king Otto I (later Otto the Great) decisively defeated the Magyar raiders near Augsburg. It ended decades of Magyar raids into Western Europe and pushed the Magyars to settle and Christianize.
